title: Who reports the income?
hook: Would third-party records change the opportunity for tax evasion?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Contrast third-party and self-reported income without treating their association as an individual moral trait.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Contrast third-party and self-reported income without treating their association as an individual moral trait.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: An illustrative income table has €1,000 and an unreported share of 0.3%. What amount is unreported? Toy inputs A=[1000, 0.3]; B=[1000, 37].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[3, 1000, 0.3], [370, 1000, 37]]. Labels: Unreported €, Income €, Unreported %.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: Reporting channel and unreported amount are separate variables. Applying two supplied rates to the same income shows their numerical contrast. It does not convert a channel-level association into an individual moral trait or a universal tax parameter.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Income €=1000, Unreported %=37. What is Unreported €? Answer: 370.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Income €=1000, Unreported %=37. What is Unreported €?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 370. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Danish tax evasion was about 0.3% of income reported by employers or banks, versus about 37% of self-reported income (Kleven et al., 2011).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Contrast third-party and self-reported income without treating their association as an individual moral trait.
